claims.text: A laser-cladded AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating containing WC particles is proposed for repairing the damaged surface.
The target component surface is prone to hot cracking because of previous repair attempts or operational stress.
Laser cladding can provide rapid heating and cooling, low dilution, and strong metallurgical bonding.
The repaired surface is intended for service involving high temperature, corrosive media, and mechanical wear.
Laser cladding produces metallurgical bonding between the HEA coating and the substrate.
Laser cladding produces a refined, fine-grained AlCoCrFeNi-WC coating microstructure.
WC particles reinforce the coating and inhibit crack initiation and propagation.
Laser cladding induces rapid solidification in the deposited HEA coating.
Rapid solidification creates fine grains that enhance coating hardness and wear resistance.
Metallurgical bonding and microstructural refinement reduce residual stresses.
Laser cladding mitigates hot-cracking hazards relative to traditional fusion welding.
The AlCoCrFeNi-WC coating improves hardness and wear resistance relative to an untreated substrate.
The repaired surface will have approximately 30–60% greater hardness than both the substrate and traditional fusion-weld repairs.
The AlCoCrFeNi-WC laser-cladded surface will have greater corrosion resistance than fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The laser-cladded repair will have a lower incidence of hot cracking than fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The improvements in hardness, wear, corrosion, and crack resistance will extend component service life under aggressive conditions.
The repair is limited to substrates capable of tolerating the thermal cycles imposed by laser cladding.
Performance depends on processing parameters, material system, and environmental severity.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires a lower incidence of hot cracking, but the falsification rule includes either a similar or reduced incidence of hot cracking within the condition said to falsify the hypothesis. A reduced incidence is a predicted success and should not count toward falsification.

The mechanism asserts that rapid laser processing reduces residual stress and hot-cracking hazards, whereas the stated rapid heating and cooling can create steep temperature gradients; the cited conflicting evidence explicitly associates those gradients with thermal stress and coating cracks. The hypothesis does not reconcile this risk through specific preheating, composition, or thermal-control conditions.
